title: Big-O Cheatsheet & Complexity Review
tagline: A complete interview-ready reference of time and space complexities for common data structures and sorting algorithms, plus a step-by-step method for analyzing any code block.

sections.content:
**Big-O notation** describes how an algorithm's resource usage grows as the input size `n` grows. It strips away constants and low-order terms to reveal the *dominant growth factor* — the one that will matter when `n` reaches millions.

In an interview, fluency with Big-O serves two purposes: (1) you can quickly discard an O(n²) brute-force and commit to an O(n log n) or O(n) solution, and (2) you can analyse a proposed solution on-the-fly and state its complexity with confidence. Neither requires memorising complex proofs — it requires recognising a handful of patterns.

This topic covers the **complexity hierarchy** from O(1) to O(n!), the **analysis method** for reading code, the **data structure operation cheatsheet** (array, hash map, linked list, stack, queue, BST, heap, trie), the **sorting algorithm cheatsheet** (bubble, insertion, merge, quick, heap, counting, radix), and the **space complexity** considerations that are easy to overlook.

flowchart TD
    A["Complexity Hierarchy\n(best to worst)"]
    A --> B["O(1) — Constant\narray index, hash lookup"]
    B --> C["O(log n) — Logarithmic\nbinary search, balanced BST"]
    C --> D["O(n) — Linear\nsingle loop, prefix sum"]
    D --> E["O(n log n) — Linearithmic\nmerge sort, heap sort"]
    E --> F["O(n²) — Quadratic\nnested loops, bubble sort"]
    F --> G["O(2ⁿ) — Exponential\nsubsets, Fibonacci naive"]
    G --> H["O(n!) — Factorial\npermutations, TSP brute force"]
sections.caption: Each tier is dramatically slower than the one above it for large n. O(log n) vs O(n) is the difference between a binary search (30 steps for 1B items) and a linear scan (1B steps).

sections.title: The Growth Rate as Distance
sections.content:
Imagine `n = 1,000,000` operations as driving from New York to Los Angeles (about 4,500 km). Now change the algorithm:

**O(1)** is teleporting — distance does not change no matter how large `n` gets. **O(log n)** is a direct flight — about 40 km of 'work' regardless of traffic. **O(n)** is driving the freeway — 4,500 km. **O(n log n)** adds a few detours — 4,600 km. Manageable.

**O(n²)** is walking the same 4,500 km route, then starting over from each kilometre — 20,000,000,000 km. You are now crossing the galaxy. **O(2ⁿ)** is entirely unthinkable for n > 60 on any hardware that exists today. These analogies are not exaggerations — for n = 1,000,000, O(n²) performs one *quintillion* operations. Modern CPUs do ~10⁹ ops/second, so that is one billion seconds — 31 years.

**Analysis method — four rules:**

**Rule 1: Drop constants.** O(2n) → O(n). O(500) → O(1). Constants reflect implementation detail, not growth rate.

**Rule 2: Drop low-order terms.** O(n² + n) → O(n²). As n grows, n² dominates completely.

**Rule 3: Sequential blocks add.** A loop of n then a loop of n is O(n + n) = O(n), not O(n²). Two sequential O(n) blocks sum to O(n).

**Rule 4: Nested blocks multiply.** A loop of n *inside* a loop of n is O(n × n) = O(n²). Three nested loops → O(n³).

**Data structure cheatsheet (access / search / insert / delete):**
- **Array (unsorted):** O(1) / O(n) / O(n) [shift] / O(n) [shift] — random access O(1), but insertions/deletions shift elements.
- **Array (sorted):** O(1) / O(log n) [binary] / O(n) / O(n) — binary search pays off, but mutations still shift.
- **Hash Map:** O(1) avg / O(1) avg / O(1) avg / O(1) avg — amortised, with O(n) worst case on collision.
- **Singly Linked List:** O(n) / O(n) / O(1) at head / O(1) at head — O(n) to reach an arbitrary node, O(1) once there.
- **Stack / Queue:** O(n) / O(n) / O(1) / O(1) — push/pop/enqueue/dequeue are O(1).
- **Binary Search Tree (balanced — AVL/Red-Black):** O(log n) for access, search, insert, delete.
- **BST (unbalanced / skewed):** degrades to O(n) — a reason to always use self-balancing variants.
- **Min/Max Heap:** O(n) access / O(n) search / O(log n) insert / O(log n) extract-min — `peek` (top) is O(1).
- **Trie:** O(m) for insert/search/delete where m = key length — ideal for prefix queries.

**Sorting cheatsheet (best / avg / worst / space):**
- **Bubble:** O(n) / O(n²) / O(n²) / O(1) — simple, rarely used in practice.
- **Insertion:** O(n) / O(n²) / O(n²) / O(1) — fast on nearly-sorted data.
- **Merge:** O(n log n) all cases / O(n) space — stable, guaranteed.
- **Quick:** O(n log n) avg / O(n²) worst / O(log n) space — in-place, fastest in practice; worst case avoidable with randomised pivot.
- **Heap:** O(n log n) all cases / O(1) space — not stable but no extra memory.
- **Counting:** O(n + k) / O(k) space — optimal when value range k is small.
- **Radix:** O(nk) / O(n + k) — sorts integers digit by digit without comparison.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Each snippet isolates one complexity class. The binary search halves the search space each iteration — 1 billion items need at most 30 iterations. Merge sort's recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to O(n log n) via the Master Theorem. The memoised Fibonacci drops from O(2ⁿ) to O(n) by caching subproblems.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **State space complexity explicitly.** Interviewers frequently ask 'What is the space complexity?' after you state the time complexity. Recursive solutions use O(depth) stack space — which is O(n) for linear recursion and O(log n) for divide-and-conquer. A hash set or map that grows with input is O(n) space. The output array also counts. Make a habit of thinking about both axes — time AND space — before presenting a solution.

items: **Drop constants and lower-order terms.** O(2n + 50) is O(n); O(n² + n) is O(n²).
**Nested loops multiply; sequential blocks add.** A loop inside a loop → O(n²); two back-to-back loops → O(n).
**Halving the input each step → O(log n).** Binary search and balanced BST operations are the canonical examples.
**Hash maps trade O(n) space for O(1) average-time lookups** — the most common brute-force-to-optimal upgrade in interviews.
**Sorting cheatsheet:** Merge sort O(n log n) guaranteed stable. Quick sort O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst. Heap sort O(n log n) O(1) space. Counting/Radix O(n) but range-limited.
**Space complexity includes the call stack.** Recursion depth n → O(n) space. Log-depth divide-and-conquer → O(log n) space.
**Prefer balanced BST (AVL/Red-Black) over a plain BST** — an unbalanced BST degrades to O(n) for all operations.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of O(3n² + 5n + 100)?
quiz.explanation: Drop the constant multiplier (3) and the lower-order terms (5n + 100). The dominant term is n², so the Big-O is O(n²).

quiz.question: A function has two separate loops, each iterating n times. What is the total time complexity?
options: O(log n) — each loop halves the work.
quiz.explanation: Sequential (non-nested) loops add: O(n) + O(n) = O(2n). Drop the constant → O(n). Multiplication only occurs when loops are nested inside each other.

quiz.question: Binary search on a sorted array of 1 billion elements requires at most how many comparisons?
quiz.explanation: Binary search is O(log₂ n). log₂(1,000,000,000) ≈ 30. Each comparison halves the remaining search space, so 30 halvings cover 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 billion items.

quiz.question: What is the average-case time complexity of hash map insert and lookup?
quiz.explanation: Hash maps achieve O(1) average-case for insert, lookup, and delete via hashing. Worst case (all keys collide to the same bucket) is O(n), but a good hash function makes this vanishingly rare.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm guarantees O(n log n) in ALL cases (best, average, and worst) with O(1) extra space?
quiz.explanation: Heap Sort is O(n log n) in all three cases and uses O(1) extra space (it sorts in-place using the heap property). Merge sort is O(n log n) always but needs O(n) space. Quick sort has O(n²) worst case.

quiz.question: A recursive function calls itself once for each element (no branching). What is its space complexity due to the call stack?
quiz.explanation: Linear recursion (no branching, one call per element) creates n stack frames before any can be freed. This is O(n) space on the call stack, regardless of what each frame does.

quiz.question: What happens to a Binary Search Tree if elements are inserted in sorted order with no rebalancing?
options: It becomes maximally balanced — sorted input is optimal for BSTs.
It degrades to a linked list, making all operations O(n).
It triggers automatic rebalancing in standard BST implementations.
It increases height to O(log n) due to the sorted property.
quiz.explanation: Inserting sorted values into a plain BST creates a completely skewed tree (every node has only a right child) — effectively a linked list. All operations degrade to O(n). AVL or Red-Black trees prevent this with rotation-based rebalancing.

quiz.question: You must check whether any value in an array of n integers appears more than once. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Sort the array then compare adjacent elements — O(n log n) time, O(1) space.
Use a Set to track seen values — O(n) time, O(n) space.
Use nested loops to compare all pairs — O(n²) time, O(1) space.
Both A and B are optimal; choose based on whether you can afford O(n) space.
quiz.explanation: Both approaches are valid and the choice is a genuine trade-off: O(n log n) time / O(1) space (sort) vs. O(n) time / O(n) space (Set). Neither dominates — this is the canonical time-space trade-off. Acknowledging both options in an interview shows maturity.

quiz.question: Counting Sort achieves O(n + k) time. What is k?
options: The log of the maximum value.
The range of possible values (max − min + 1).
quiz.explanation: Counting Sort allocates a frequency array of size k = (max − min + 1). It is linear when k is small relative to n (e.g., sorting ages 0–120 or characters 0–255). When k >> n, it becomes wasteful.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of inserting a key into a Min-Heap of n elements?
quiz.explanation: Inserting into a heap appends the new element to the end of the array and then 'bubbles up' by swapping with parent nodes until the heap property is restored. In the worst case this traverses the full height of the tree: O(log n).
